evals.prompt: I run developer relations at Meridian Stack, an infrastructure company with about 40 engineers. Every month I send leadership the same five numbers: total GitHub stars (11,400), blog impressions (roughly 90k), Twitter followers (8,900), cumulative npm downloads (2.1M) and conferences attended (9 so far this year). Our VP of Engineering replied to the last one asking 'what is any of this actually for?' and I didn't have a good answer. Can you put together something better for me to send next month?
evals.expected_output: A measurement framework with five to eight metrics, each carrying definition, source, baseline, threshold, owner and action, a written attribution rule, a blind-spots section and a kill rule. The four cumulative totals are rejected as monotonic and either converted to period deltas or cut; the conference count is named as an activity log rather than an outcome.
expectations: Identifies total GitHub stars (11,400) as a monotonic metric that cannot fall, and refuses it as a primary metric
Applies the same monotonic objection to cumulative npm downloads (2.1M) and to the Twitter follower count (8,900)
Names the conference-attendance count (9) as a record of effort rather than an outcome
The resulting metric sheet holds between five and eight metrics
At least one metric in the sheet sits in the product-impact or business-impact tier
Every metric row carries all six fields: definition, source, baseline, threshold, owner and action
States that npm download counts are HTTP request counts including CI and mirror traffic, not people
Produces a written attribution rule as a section distinct from the metric sheet
Includes a non-empty known-blind-spots section
States a kill rule removing any metric that has not changed a decision in two consecutive review cycles
Does not deliver tracking instrumentation, an event taxonomy or analytics code as the answer
Labels each threshold with where it came from, using sourced, baseline or hypothesis
Does not compare the 11,400 stars against another company's star count as a benchmark

evals.prompt: Calderon Labs here, Series B, we sell a data-pipeline product. I have to pick what to instrument first for our developer program and I want to get the order right rather than boiling the ocean. Useful context: we already run Amplitude across the product and it's clean, we have roughly two engineering days I can borrow this quarter, and our sales ops lead has flatly refused to open CRM fields to us or to anyone outside the revenue team. Where do I start and in what order?
evals.expected_output: A build order derived from value per unit of effort rather than from cost, putting enablement first and reach last, with influenced pipeline deleted outright because sales ops will not cooperate and recorded in the blind-spots section with the cost of closing it. The existing product-analytics install is named as the answer that promotes enablement and product impact.
expectations: States the build order is decided by value per unit of effort, not by cost of collection
Places enablement first as the best value-per-effort ratio on the ladder
Places reach last despite it being the cheapest tier to collect
Gives the efficiency ordering as enablement, then engagement, then product impact, then business impact, then reach
Deletes influenced pipeline outright because sales ops will not share data, rather than demoting it or ranking it last
Records the deleted business-impact metric in the blind-spots section together with what it would take to obtain it
Promotes enablement and product impact because product analytics is already instrumented
Names which answer from the user moved which tier
States that value and collection effort both rise down the tier ladder, so the ladder alone does not answer what to build first
Sets the default primary metric at the enablement tier
Does not recommend starting with reach metrics on the grounds that they are already available
Does not present the five-tier ladder to the user as an industry standard model

evals.prompt: Growth engineer at Thistledown, we make a TypeScript SDK for payments reconciliation. Our head of DevRel wants to know which channels bring developers in, and my plan was to put UTM parameters on absolutely everything - every talk slide QR code, every repo link, every newsletter - and then report channel totals from that. I have about three hours a week for this. Does that plan hold up, and what would you do first?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation to stand up self-reported attribution first as the standing instrument, with tagged links restricted to comparing artifacts of the same type and never used for program totals, plus the efficiency ordering of the four methods, the stated bias of each, and the instruction to write the rule before the period starts.
expectations: Recommends self-reported attribution, a single question at signup, as the first method to stand up
Gives the efficiency ordering of methods as self-reported, then pre/post lift, then tagged links, then influenced pipeline
Restricts tagged links to comparing artifacts of the same type and forbids using them for program totals
States that self-reported attribution is the only method that sees hallway conversations, podcasts and colleague recommendations
Names the bias of self-reported attribution: over-counts memorable touches, under-counts docs and search
Specifies exactly one question, with an option list held stable across quarters
Keeps a free-text option in the question so unlisted channels surface
Reports the result as self-reported first touch rather than as attribution
States that a large direct bucket is normal rather than a tracking defect
Cites roughly 70% of AI-assistant traffic arriving with no referrer, and marks the figure as directional rather than measured
States the attribution rule must be written before the period starts, not after it
Notes that the marginal effort of pre/post lift is recording the pre-period before the push, which is impossible afterwards

evals.prompt: Hollowbrook, we sell an observability platform, mostly six-figure enterprise deals with an 8-month average cycle. Our CRO stood up at the QBR and said DevRel sourced $1.2M last quarter based on a spreadsheet someone put together after the fact by looking at which closed accounts had been to one of our workshops. He now wants that number every quarter and he wants me to own it. I'd rather have something I can actually defend. How do I write this down?
evals.expected_output: A written influenced-pipeline rule naming touch types, a lookback window and a stage condition, fixed for the fiscal year, with sourced credit refused throughout, shared credit stated, retroactively recorded touches excluded, the leading indicator for the enterprise latency named, and the revenue-metric decision made deliberately against who owns the budget.
expectations: Refuses the word sourced and uses influenced throughout
States that Marketing and Sales may claim the same opportunities and that shared credit is inherent to the metric
The rule names which touch types count as a program touch
The rule names an explicit lookback window in days
The rule names whether the touch must precede a specific pipeline stage
States the rule is fixed for the fiscal year and that any mid-period change must be reported as a restatement
Excludes any touch recorded after the opportunity was created
States the metric over-counts by construction because engaged accounts were already more likely to buy, and that this is stated once rather than re-argued each quarter
Names a leading indicator to carry the interim, given enterprise cycles push the pipeline answer two to four quarters out
Flags influenced pipeline as carrying the highest compliance cost because it joins a named person's community activity to a CRM record
Presents both defensible positions on the revenue question: no sales metrics on DevRel with the DevRel Qualified Lead as the alternative currency, and influenced pipeline explicitly shared
States the deciding input for that choice is who owns the budget

evals.prompt: I maintain Quillmark, an Apache-2.0 document toolchain with 4,200 stars and about 30 recurring contributors. There is no company and nothing to sell. Our steering committee wants a health report every quarter and someone on the list told us CHAOSS says first response within 24 hours is the standard we should hold ourselves to. What should we actually be measuring, and is that 24-hour figure right?
evals.expected_output: The CHAOSS Starter Project Health set adopted by definition, with the correction that CHAOSS publishes no numeric target for any of its four metrics, the two-business-day figure attributed to VMware rather than CHAOSS, the 24-hour figure labelled folklore, thresholds derived from the project's own baseline, and stars cut in favour of downloads, dependents and unique cloners.
expectations: Anchors the framework on the CHAOSS Starter Project Health metric set rather than inventing a metric list
Names all four CHAOSS starter metrics: time to first response, change-request closure ratio, contributor absence factor, release frequency
Corrects the user by stating CHAOSS publishes no numeric target for any of the four metrics
Identifies the two-business-day first-response figure as VMware's internal guideline quoted inside a case study, not a CHAOSS standard
Labels the 24-hour first-response figure as folklore or a hypothesis under test rather than a standard
Defines time to first response as the first human response, with bots excluded
Defines change-request closure ratio as closed, meaning merged plus rejected, divided by opened in the same window
Defines contributor absence factor as the smallest number of people producing 50% of contributions
Adopts the CHAOSS definitions verbatim while deriving every threshold from the project's own trailing baseline
Refuses to compare the project against other projects' published numbers
Recommends downloads, dependents or unique cloners over the 4,200 stars as the adoption signal
Notes that bot and automation activity distorts time to first response and change-request closure ratio
States that GitHub's repository traffic endpoints retain only 14 days of data and require write access, so snapshotting must start the day the metric enters the sheet
Cuts the star count rather than keeping it as a primary metric, on the grounds that stars are gameable and not comparable across project types

evals.prompt: Head of DevRel at Vantablue, we make a CI orchestration tool. I have four advocates and I want everyone clear on what good looks like, so I drafted individual quarterly targets: 6 blog posts per month each, 40 community messages per week each, 20 GitHub issues closed per month each, and 500 signups per quarter attributed to each person. Comp is going to be partly tied to these. Can you sanity-check the set and tell me what I'm missing?
evals.expected_output: Each incentivised volume target paired with a named counter-metric, the specific degradations each target produces spelled out, per-person targets rejected in favour of measuring the program, and the three anti-vanity tests applied with failing metrics cut rather than softened.
expectations: Pairs every incentivised volume metric with a counter-metric
Pairs the blog-post count with organic entries per post
Pairs closed issues with reopen rate
Pairs signups with 30-day retention
Cites the formulation that when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure, attributed to Marilyn Strathern's 1997 generalisation of Goodhart's law
Names the specific degradations the targets produce: thin posts, premature issue closes, low-value chatter and throwaway accounts
Rejects per-person metric targets and measures the program rather than the individual
States that per-person targets turn colleagues into competitors and pull work toward whatever is counted
Applies the so-what test by naming the action each surviving metric triggers, and cutting any metric with no action
Applies the ownership test, asking whether this team's work can plausibly move the number within one review period
Applies the monotonic test to the candidate metrics
Caps the resulting sheet at no more than eight metrics
Cuts a metric that fails any of the three tests rather than softening or rewording it

evals.prompt: Ferrowind, we sell a Rust-based edge runtime. Last month we had 11 enterprise conversations at a conference versus 4 the month before, which I've been writing up as 175% growth, and external pull requests went from 2 to 6. Last month was also the month we shipped 2.0 and did the Show HN. Separately, a competitor's engineering blog says they take 300 external PRs a year, and my CEO has started quoting that at me. Help me put together the monthly report.
evals.expected_output: The small-N counts reported as raw dated lists rather than percentages, the conference-plus-launch month identified as a burst and refused as a trend, the competitor's absolute figure refused as a benchmark in favour of the program's own history, and thresholds deferred until three prior periods exist.
expectations: Refuses to express the 11 versus 4 enterprise conversations as a percentage or rate, and requires the raw list with dates instead
Applies the same treatment to the 6 versus 2 external pull requests
States the small-N floor at roughly 30 events in a period, below which a rate should not be reported
Labels that 30-event floor as a borrowed rule of thumb rather than a DevRel-measured cutoff
Identifies the conference plus the 2.0 launch and Show HN as a burst rather than a trend
Refuses to present the launch month against the prior quiet month as a trend line
Refuses to benchmark the program against the competitor's 300 external pull requests as an absolute number
States the correct comparison is the program against its own past
Names why cross-company absolute comparison fails: differences in audience size, ecosystem and product maturity
Requires at least three prior periods of history before any threshold is set
Sets targets as a direction and a range for the first two cycles rather than a point value
Does not report or endorse the 175% growth figure

evals.prompt: Nordholm, we ship client libraries for a geospatial API in three languages. Two numbers I put on the board deck every quarter: 240,000 docs sessions from Google Analytics, and total monthly package downloads of 305,000, which is npm at 180k plus PyPI at 95k plus crates.io at 30k. I describe the second one as monthly users. Our new CTO poked at both last week. Are they defensible, and if not what do I replace them with?
evals.expected_output: Both numbers rejected: registry downloads are request counts that cannot be summed across registries or called users, and the Google Analytics session count is a large undercount of a developer audience. Replacements are step-to-step ratios measured inside a single source, with each definition written beside its number.
expectations: Rejects calling 305,000 downloads users, and states registry downloads are request counts rather than people
States npm counts every HTTP 200 tarball response, including continuous integration and mirror traffic
States PyPI excludes known mirrors by default, so the two registries are not measured on the same basis
Refuses to sum downloads across registries and present the total as users
Flags the 240,000 Google Analytics docs sessions as a substantial undercount for a developer audience
Cites the Plausible measurement of 58% of a tech audience blocking Google Analytics, 82.3% on Linux and 88.3% on Firefox
Qualifies that measurement with its scope: one site, August 2021, traffic skewed toward Hacker News and Reddit
Requires reach and engagement metrics be built as ratios inside one source rather than as absolutes compared across sources
Does not retain an absolute session count as a headline metric
Notes npm treats under roughly 50 downloads per day as mostly automation
Requires the definition of each number to be written next to the number
Requires any surviving reach metric to have a named downstream partner in the same row's story or be dropped

evals.prompt: Saltmarsh Data, 3-person developer relations team - one on docs, one advocate, one running the community. Our charter names two funded goals for the year. I want the framework built this week. I've been reading up and I'd like us to track the AAARRRP stages and also map where developers are dropping off across the journey, so we get both views. Give me the framework.
evals.expected_output: An explicit brainstorming pass offering two or three whole spines with their sources, what each makes visible and hides, who it is legible to and when it is the wrong pick, a recommendation with reasons, a refusal to stack AAARRRP with journey stages, and no metric sheet written until the owner picks a spine.
expectations: States explicitly that it is in brainstorming mode before offering anything
Offers two or three whole spines rather than a single framework
Names driver-anchored AAARRRP, journey-stage, and the awareness/enablement/engagement function split among the options
Attributes AAARRRP to Phil Leggetter in 2016, adapted from Dave McClure's AARRR with a seventh element for developer products
Attributes the awareness, enablement and engagement split to Mary Thengvall
Attributes the developer-journey stage model to Matthew Revell
Presents each spine with what it makes visible, what it hides, who it is legible to, and the conditions under which it is the wrong pick
Recommends one spine and states why
Refuses to run AAARRRP and journey stages together, naming double-counting of the same work as the reason
Does not rank the spines by an efficiency or value-per-effort ratio
States the deciding criterion is the spine the funder can already read
Ranks the tiers underneath the chosen spine instead of ranking the spines
Does not write the metric sheet before the owner has picked a spine
Presents the framework one section at a time and seeks agreement before continuing

evals.prompt: Brackenridge, we launched our developer platform three months ago so there's very little history. Our PM has drafted the OKRs for next quarter and wants to lock them tomorrow: 40% seven-day retention because that's the industry standard, a 20% monthly-active ratio, 30% self-serve activation which she says is typical for devtools, and first response within 24 hours on community questions. She wants me to sign off. Should I?
evals.expected_output: Each of the four figures identified as folklore or an unsourced practitioner claim and refused as a target, every threshold tagged with its provenance in the same cell, metrics marked baselining given three months of history, and targets expressed as a direction and a range with a baseline-relative threshold preferred over a fixed line.
expectations: Labels the 40% seven-day retention figure as folklore or a hypothesis rather than a benchmark
Labels the 20% monthly-active ratio as folklore
Labels the 20-40% self-serve activation band as a practitioner claim rather than a study, covering the PM's 30% figure
Labels the 24-hour first-response figure as folklore
Refuses to set any of the four as a target
Requires every threshold to be tagged sourced, baseline or hypothesis in the same cell as the number
States that almost every threshold should be self-set from the program's own trailing baseline
Requires at least three prior periods before any threshold is set
Marks metrics lacking history as baselining and defers their thresholds to the next review
States that an exec who discovers one invented benchmark discounts every other figure on the page
Sets targets as a direction and a range for the first two cycles rather than a point value
Prefers a threshold that moves with the baseline, such as two standard deviations from a 30-day rolling mean, over a fixed line
Labels the three-period, two-standard-deviation and 30-day-window figures as borrowed conventions rather than DevRel-measured values
Does not present any of the four circulating numbers as sourced or published

evals.prompt: Kestrel Logic, we make an embedded database. Four things landed on me this week and I need help across all of them. Our Discord has 2,100 members and feels dead, and I need to know if it actually is. Our UTM parameters are a mess and the GitHub traffic panel disagrees with our analytics tool on every number. We spent 40k on a DevRelCon booth in March and finance wants to know what it returned. And underneath all of that, our CTO has asked what the developer program should be reporting to her every quarter. Where do we start?
evals.expected_output: The three off-scope asks routed to the named sibling skills using owner/repo@skill references, only the program-wide quarterly reporting question kept in scope, no tracking plan or community dashboard produced, metric selection stated as preceding instrumentation, and pre-conditions named per metric with any failing metric handed off as an instrumentation request.
expectations: Routes the Discord health question to samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-community-health
Routes the UTM and tool-disagreement question to samber/developer-relations-skills@devrel-analytics
Routes the 40k booth return question to samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-event-sponsorship
Keeps only the program-wide quarterly reporting question in scope for itself
Does not produce an event taxonomy, UTM convention or tracking plan as its deliverable
Does not produce a community-only health dashboard as its deliverable
States that choosing which metrics to report comes before instrumenting them
Hands any metric the team cannot instrument to samber/developer-relations-skills@devrel-analytics as a gap rather than assuming it away
Uses the owner/repo@skill reference format when naming each routed skill
States the pre-conditions each metric needs before it can enter the sheet
Calls a metric that fails its pre-conditions an instrumentation request rather than a metric
Distinguishes deciding which metrics deserve a target from making them collectable

evals.prompt: Ashcombe, developer tooling company. I defend our budget in five weeks in front of the CMO, who signs off on our headcount - we sit on the marketing line. I have zero engineering days available between now and then; the platform team is frozen on a migration. We have never recorded a pre-period for anything. I want to put cohort retention of developers we've touched on the slide, going back over the last three quarters, and I can tag the cohort retroactively from our event attendee lists. What should the slide say?
evals.expected_output: The retroactive cohort refused because cohorts must be defined before the period, the five-week deadline used to promote engagement and enablement and demote anything needing a pre-period, every metric requiring new instrumentation deleted given zero engineering days and handed to devrel-analytics, business impact promoted ahead of its efficiency ratio because the reader renews the budget and the program sits on the marketing line, and no sourced revenue promised.
expectations: Refuses to build cohort retention from a retroactively tagged cohort
States that a cohort must be defined before the period starts, not after
Promotes engagement and enablement because the deadline sits inside one quarter
Demotes or excludes anything requiring a pre-period that does not already exist
States that a metric taking two quarters to instrument does nothing for a budget review five weeks away
Deletes every metric that needs a newly instrumented event, given zero engineering days available
Hands the resulting instrumentation gap to samber/developer-relations-skills@devrel-analytics
Names which of the user's answers moved which tier
Promotes business impact ahead of its efficiency ratio because the reader decides budget renewal and the program is funded from the marketing line
Asks whether the user needs a one-off win at that date or a sheet that still reads in a year
Specifies cohorts by month rather than by day
Does not promise sourced revenue or last-touch revenue attribution on the slide
Names a leading indicator to carry the interim for any lagging business-impact metric
